subject: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
posts: Massive digital infrastructure promises local booms, but do data centers actually deliver the jobs communities are promised? #DataCenters #Economy 🌐
Proponents claim data centers spark explosive local economic transformation and widespread employment. Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good
Research on 1,584 facilities reveals modest job gains (1,000-1,300 per county after 3-5 years) alongside heavy water/power drain. Resulting Judgement: (+0.20, -0.20) — Lesser Good

Verdict: PASS — Fall from Grace.
Empirical research replaces speculative hype with grounded economic accounting.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.1, z: 1)
Researchers analyzed 1,584 U.S. data centers opened between 2000 and 2023, comparing county employment trends before and after facility launches.

The Poison:
Heavy utility strains, water consumption, and tax breaks often offset modest local employment gains.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing massive capital investment (WHAT) with broad local labor impact (WHO).

Social Physics Analysis:
Communities face a smart selfish squeeze where developers leverage tax breaks for capital-heavy servers while local grids bear high power and water costs.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall from Grace.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> May be via Destructive Geodesic. Stated utopian expansion tempers into measured reality.

The Unavoidable Truth: Data centers do stimulate localized support jobs after a multi-year lag.
The Unavoidable Lie: Every host county experiences an instant economic miracle.

Alethekanon:
Capital-intensive infrastructure requires rigorous empirical accounting rather than speculative hype.

Awwthekanon:
It's tough when communities hope for a windfall only to get high electric bills and a quiet server farm.

Brothekanon:
Turns out racks of servers don't turn a small town into Silicon Valley overnight.

Spirithekanon:
"Better is a handful with quietness than both hands full together, grasping for the wind." Ecclesiastes 4:6 PASS
Sustained local well-being outvalues speculative economic frenzies.

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth ===

[Source 1 — theconversation.com] (URL: https://theconversation.com/we-studied-1-584-data-centers-and-found-the-buildings-full-of-machines-are-tied-to-modest-local-job-growth-293872):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth

This employment boost took three to five years to show up, two researchers found after studying more than two decades of data.

Actual Article Body:
Share article

Print article

Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return.

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction, from Ohio to Texas. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.

Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.

First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.

Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.

Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.

The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.

By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.

Assistant Professor of Finance, Miami University

Professor of Urban and Real Estate Economics, York University, Canada

A rare black-colored red fox, shown in Northbrook in recent years.

Jeff Nelson

Share

A rare black-colored red fox that’s been spotted in Northbrook for at least a year or two was recently found dead, according to wildlife officials who are awaiting test results to get a better picture of why it died.

Before its demise, the creature suffered some sort of physical trauma along the lines of getting hit by a car, said Cook County Forest Preserves wildlife biologist Chris Anchor.

But it also exhibited signs of other underlying health issues, he said, adding that more tests are being completed.

“Very sad,” Anchor said. “It’s a very charismatic animal, a beautiful animal.”

Northbrook’s black fox

Jeff Nelson

Two red foxes, one orange and the other black, shown in Northbrook.

Jeff Nelson

A black red fox appears to be posing for a photo in Northbrook.

Jeff Nelson

The “melanistic” red fox, shown with a ground utility marker.

Jeff Nelson

Gina Manski, the north suburb’s animal control officer, said she got a call Oct. 9 of a dead black fox or coyote in a yard. Before even seeing it, she knew it was a fox, as it was a relatively well-known occupant of the community that had intrigued and puzzled residents for some time.

“I was very, very, very sad, I can tell you that,” Manski said about the fox’s death. “There were a lot of people who were sad. Hopefully he mated and passed that gene on.”

The animal is believed to be the same fox written about in August by the Chicago Sun-Times, which noted the coloration is the result of a rare genetic quirk. Foxes like this are called “melanistic” because they have elevated levels of melanin that determines pigmentation.

Most red foxes are — given the name of the breed — reddish in color, skewing orange.

Preliminary tests found the fox had signs of a parasitic infection and an enlarged heart, among other problems. Anchor said studying why some wild creatures die is important so experts can detect trends in disease that can impact wildlife and, sometimes, humans.

While some people are alarmed upon seeing a fox, Manski said they’re usually not bothersome to humans and “provide a service by eating a lot of rodents, especially mice.”

While they’re certainly not immune from vehicle strikes, a 2007 British study suggested red foxes in an urban environment overseas “appeared to reduce the mortality risk of minor category roads by changing ... activity patterns.”

There have been other black foxes in the Chicago region. A black-colored red fox kit was spotted in far southwest suburban Lockport in 2024.

Single mom found dead at bottom of Kansas bridge may have suffered shocking ‘tragic accident’

A Kansas mom of two has been found dead after failing to return home from her morning walk – and cops are now investigating if she fell through a gap on a bridge.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A single mom of two was mysteriously found dead at the bottom of a Kansas bridge — with cops now fearing she may have slipped through a gap in a “tragic accident.”

Monica Rivera, 24, was last seen on a morning walk along Kansas City’s 7th Street bridge early Friday when she suddenly vanished, getting reported missing later that day, police said.

A body was then found later that morning in an industrial area underneath the bridge, which was later confirmed to be the missing mom.

The preliminary autopsy indicated “no evidence of foul play” — and the alarming theory is that the mom accidentally slipped through a known gap in the bridge decking.

“It kind of looks like it’s one continuous deck … but there’s actually a gap,” police spokesperson Nancy Chartrand told the Kansas City Star, describing Rivera’s death as a “tragic accident.”

“If you were trying to go from one side to the other, you could possibly fall.”

Rivera’s grieving family says she died “due to a safety oversight” – with her aunt, Cassie Bennett, creating a Change.org petition urging the city to take action.

The aunt claimed the city has not addressed the fault “despite repeated concerns raised by the community.”

“This fatal accident could have been avoided if the city had taken timely action to ensure the safety of its citizens,” she said.

“The neglect of this apparent flaw goes against these standards and must be rectified immediately.

“By addressing this gap, we can prevent further accidents and ensure our loved ones are safe when they traverse this bridge.”

The single mom, from Wyandotte County, has been described by her heartbroken pals online as someone with a “beautiful” soul.

“Fly high & stay dancing in the sky. Thank you for being a friend,” pal Crystal Lynn said of Rivera.
